name: Repeated-chord motor
description: the engine of the driving movements. Straight eighths or sixteenths on one chord: `[C3,Eb3,G3]e ×8`. Relentless, and it *accumulates*: what makes it Beethoven rather than Alberti is that it does not decorate, it insists. Use under a melody that is itself agitated.

name: Broken octaves / murky bass
description: `C2s C3s C2s C3s …`. The storm engine (Op.13 first movement, Op.31/2). Wider and heavier than a tremolo; the two notes are an octave apart and the effect is a low growl, not a shimmer.

name: Rising bass line against a static melody
description: quarters or half notes climbing chromatically or by step while the right hand holds: `C2h C#2h`, `D2h Eb2h`. This is how Beethoven builds tension without getting louder, and it is almost absent from generated writing.

name: The LH takes the theme
description: the motif moves to the bass while the right hand accompanies. Not a device to save for a fugue: it happens constantly in the sonatas, usually at the start of a development. If the piece has a theme and the bass never states it, that is a missed opportunity in every movement.

name: Sforzando punctuation on a weak beat
description: `rest_q [C2,C3]q:sfz rest_h`. A single loud stab where the metre does not expect one. One of the most recognisable Beethoven fingerprints and it costs one note.

name: Octave doubling of the melody
description: both hands on the same line, two or three octaves apart, for a bare unison statement. Use at a theme's most emphatic return, and at the opening of a movement that means to sound severe.

name: Sustained low octave under everything
description: `[C1,C2]w` held for two or four bars while the right hand works above. The bottom of the piano used as a *pedal point*, not as a bass line. Enormous weight for one note.

name: Alberti, deliberately plain
description: `C3e G3e E3e G3e ×2`. Beethoven inherits it and uses it sparingly, usually in an early or a lyrical work. If a whole movement is Alberti it is Mozart's costume, not Beethoven's.

name: Silence
description: `rest_w`. The left hand stops. Beethoven drops the bass out before a return, before a fortissimo, and at the moment a phrase is meant to hang. A whole bar of nothing underneath is a device, not a gap.

name: Contrary-motion scales
description: both hands moving apart or together in scales (`C3e D3e E3e F3e G3e A3e B3e C4e` against a descending right hand). Used at transitions and in codas; it is *motion* rather than accompaniment.

name: Widely-spaced arpeggios
description: the hand covering two octaves per bar: `C2e G2e C3e E3e G3e C4e G3e E3e`. Open, resonant, and characteristic of the later sonatas. Compare with Alberti's narrow oscillation.

name: Off-beat chords with a silent downbeat
description: `rest_e [Eb3,G3]e [Eb3,G3]e [Eb3,G3]e …`. The bar has no floor under its first beat. Unsettling in exactly the way Beethoven likes.

name: Alberti bass
when_to_use: Simple support (stay out of melody's way)

name: Murky bass (octave alternation)
when_to_use: Simple support (stay out of melody's way)

name: Waltz bass (3/4, L:1/8)
when_to_use: Simple support (stay out of melody's way)

name: The tiny cell
description: a motif of three or four notes, often only a rhythm. Everything grows from it. Write the cell first, then build the theme out of repetitions of it.

name: Motivic fragmentation
description: the theme is stated, then only its first half, then only its first bar, then only its rhythm. Progressive shortening builds tension better than anything else in the vocabulary.

name: Sforzando on a weak beat
description: `C5q:sfz` on beat 2 or 4, or off the beat entirely. Displaces the metre without changing it. One of the most reliable Beethoven fingerprints.

name: Syncopation across the barline
description: a note tied from the last beat of one bar into the next, so the downbeat is not attacked. Sustained over several bars it makes the metre genuinely ambiguous.

name: Sudden dynamic contradiction
description: `ff` followed immediately by `p` with no transition, or a long crescendo that arrives at `pp`. The second is the more characteristic and the more startling.

name: Repeated-note insistence
description: the same pitch struck three, four, six times. Not decoration; it is the argument refusing to move on.

name: The long crescendo over a pedal
description: eight to sixteen bars of intensification over an unchanging bass, arriving at a structural downbeat.

name: Registral extremes juxtaposed
description: a phrase in the deep bass answered immediately two octaves up, with nothing in between.

name: Silence as a downbeat
description: a general pause where the ear expects the strongest beat of the phrase. A whole bar of nothing, then the answer.

name: Trill as an event, not an ornament
description: a long trill sustained over several bars, usually before a return. In the late works it becomes a texture.

name: Accelerating rhythmic values
description: quarters, then eighths, then triplets, then sixteenths across a passage. Acceleration without a tempo change.

name: The wrong-note accent
description: a strong beat carrying a chromatic note that is not in the harmony, marked `sfz`, resolving afterwards.

name: Deceptive cadence, then a second attempt
description: V goes to vi, the phrase starts its cadence again, and only the third attempt lands. Extends a close from two bars to eight.

name: The flattened sixth as a shock
description: ♭VI arriving in place of an expected chord, usually loud and usually at a structural point.

name: Third-related keys
description: moving to the mediant or submediant rather than the dominant. A whole second subject in the mediant is characteristic of the middle and late works.

name: Diminished seventh as a pivot
description: the ambiguous chord used to leave a key abruptly and arrive somewhere remote.

name: Prolonged dominant preparation
description: sixteen or more bars on the dominant before a recapitulation, so the return feels earned rather than scheduled.

name: Neapolitan approach at a moment of pathos
description: ♭II6 before the dominant, in a minor-key slow movement.

name: The false return
description: the theme comes back in the wrong key or too early, and is corrected.

name: Coda as a second development
description: the coda is not a wind-down but the movement's real climax, longer than the exposition's closing group.

name: Thematic transformation across movements
description: the same cell appears in a later movement in a different character. In a multi-movement work this is what makes it one work.
